query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A machine learning‐based predictive framework that incorporates descriptors of local chemical disorder—such as mass variance, electronegativity differences, and inferred force‐constant fluctuations—can reliably identify single‐phase high-entropy alloys with ultra-low phonon thermal conductivity, outperforming traditional DFT/empirical methods in accuracy and speed.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys with four or more principal elements (e.g., equiatomic FeCoCrMnNi) in a well-mixed single-phase state that display modest force-constant fluctuations similar to binary alloys.
generation.intervention: Apply the predictive framework trained on binary/ternary alloy datasets using descriptors that quantify atomic-scale disorder and bonding fluctuations, and then extend it to screen high-entropy alloy compositions.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted at ambient to moderate temperatures (up to ~500 K) in alloys that remain structurally homogeneous (i.e., without significant phase segregation or clustering).
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical disorder manifested as mass, size, and electronegativity differences between constituent atoms, leading to force-constant fluctuations that enhance phonon scattering.
generation.mechanism: The approach works by correlating detailed atomic descriptors with enhanced phonon scattering mechanisms. By capturing how local disorder decreases phonon lifetimes, the model predicts alloys with suppressed lattice thermal conductivity—similar to observed behavior where force-constant fluctuations in HEAs reduce phonon propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method will identify HEA compositions with lattice thermal conductivity reduced by at least 20–30% compared to predictions from conventional DFT or empirical rules, closely matching experimentally measured values (e.g., approaching the low phonon conduction thresholds reported in benchmark materials).
generation.baseline: Current DFT and empirical models that require extensive computational resources and often show only moderate prediction accuracy for lattice thermal conductivity in HEAs.
generation.boundary: This predictive approach is expected to be effective only for single-phase, homogeneously mixed HEAs; its accuracy might degrade in multi-phase or segregated systems where local chemical environments deviate significantly from those in the training data.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement is uncertain due to variations in descriptor sensitivity and the limitations of training data; predictions may be less reliable in systems with unexpected local clustering or ordering that alter phonon scattering.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of HEA samples identified by the predictive model to have low lattice thermal conductivity. Perform inelastic neutron scattering to assess phonon lifetimes and use Green–Kubo or direct thermal conductivity measurements at room temperature (and up to ~500 K). Compare experimental κL values and phonon attenuation rates with model predictions.
measurements: Phonon lifetime/attenuation rates from scattering experiments
Characterization of local chemical disorder (e.g., via atom probe tomography)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If experimental measurements reveal lattice thermal conductivity values that are over 20–30% higher than predicted, or if the anticipated correlation between the calculated disorder descriptors and the phonon scattering rates is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This work shed light on the effect of constituent elements on local chemical fluctuation and lattice thermal conductivity in high-entropy thermoelectric materials and also revealed the direct relationship between the fluctuation and atomic characteristic of elements, which could serve as a guide for tailoring local chemical fluctuation in the community of high-entropy materials.

Recently, entropy engineering has been used as a novel strategy to optimize the electrical and thermal transport properties of TE materials. By increasing element species, the mixing entropy in a material system increases quickly, and high-entropy materials with over five principal elements will be formed. Severe lattice distortion is usually the core phenomenon of high-entropy material—such distortion leads to strong scattering for heat-carrying phonons and results in low lattice thermal conductivity. Stabilizing single-phase structures by increasing entropy weakens the phase-boundary electron scattering in multiphase high-entropy material, thus providing a beneficial contribution to improve electrical transport properties, i.e., entropy-driven structural stabilization,. Therefore, the high-entropy-stabilized composition should work as a good matrix for further optimization of TE performance by integrating the traditional optimization strategy.

In conclusion, we have reported the first experimental investigation of the acoustic phonon dispersions in a High-Entropy Alloy, complemented by the GVDOS survey, at room and low temperature. FeCoCrMnNi is a 5-element random alloy, and, despite the inherent disorder, its phonon dynamics closely resemble that of the pure elements composing it and the corresponding binary alloys. More specifically, acoustic phonons disperse throughout the whole Brillouin zone up to energies between 20 and 30 meV, exhibiting an attenuation stronger than in simple elements, but of the same order of magnitude as in binary alloys. The whole attenuation behavior can be understood in terms of scattering from force-constant fluctuations, which have been estimated to amount to ~20% using a simple theoretical model, a value comparable with calculations of Mu and co-authors on binary and ternary alloys made of the same elements. If this is unexpected from Mu’s theory, which would predict increased force-constant fluctuations due to the larger variability of random environments of a given atomic pair, it explains recent experimental reports on comparable phonon lattice thermal conductivities in our HEA and FeNi
